newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori hopeful after crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori hopeful after crisis talks.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday he was "optimistic" for a bloodless end to the two-month Lima hostage crisis despite the apparent lack of progress in renewed talks with Marxist rebels.

"We never foresaw that (the siege) was going to take so many days, but we are optimistic about finding a peaceful solution," Fujimori told reporters during a visit to the Amazon jungle region of Loreto in northeastern Peru.

Three rounds of face-to-face talks at a Red Cross safe house between Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) No. 2 Rolly Rojas and government negotiator Domingo Palermo raised hopes of a breakthrough after weeks without direct dialogue.

But they brought no sign that they were getting any closer on two apparently intractable positions -- MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini's demand that 400 jailed comrades be freed and Fujimori's refusal to consider this.

The Vatican's representative, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, said on Monday he and other talks "guarantors" from Canada and the Red Cross were merely working on proposals "to enable the continuation of the conversations."

Without going into detail, Fujimori said the government was making "very big efforts so that the negotiations advance," but "naturally at the beginning there are difficulties that we hope to gradually overcome."

He added that patience was needed in the negotiations between Palermo, "who goes in with arguments of a legal nature, arguments of international law", and the MRTA whose "position is one of force, threatening the lives of 72 hostages."
The two sides last met on Saturday.

Fujimori, who has floated the possibility of giving the rebels asylum abroad, added that "we should exhaust all efforts possible to find a peaceful solution" and insisted the crisis had not knocked his country's progress off track.

In its 62nd day on Monday, the crisis has become Latin America's longest hostage siege, overtaking Colombia's M-19 rebels who held 57 captives for 61 days at the Dominican Embassy in 1980 before taking $2 million and a plane to Cuba.

In Lima, Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer was less upbeat than Fujimori about the crisis, warning of health emergencies "at any moment" among the mainly middle-aged and increasingly ailing captives under rebel guns since Dec. 17.
Costa Bauer said in a radio interview some of the hostages in Lima required permanent, close monitoring, for which a special medical team had been set up.

"It is possible that emergencies might happen at any moment," he said, mentioning in particular government legislator Gilberto Siura, former Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja "and two or three others."

Siura is being treated for cancer and Pantoja wrote recently to his family that he could hardly walk. "When I do, I lose my balance. My feet, hands and fingers have all gone hard. My arthritis stops me from reading and I can barely write," his message said.
Aid workers and police say the captives' ailments include hypertension, digestive problems, asthma and depression.

With talks off, Monday began with the now-familiar broadcast from the residence of an MRTA revolutionary hymn commemorating fallen comrades. Half an hour later, police outside responded by blaring local "criollo" music -- with guitar rhythms and patriotic lyrics -- from loudspeakers aimed at the compound.

According to an army intelligence memorandum obtained on Monday by Reuters, the Peruvian military has developed a plan for a commando raid on the compound to end the siege, but it would likely result in heavy casualties.

According to the plan, U.S. and Peruvian commandos would drop onto the roof of the Japanese ambassador's home on a moonless night, plant explosives in six points and end the siege in just seven minutes. Casualties could be as high as 90 people, including three-quarters of the 72 men being held, almost all the hostage-takers and 20 commandos.
The military card, therefore, should only be played if negotiations fail, said the memo, dated Feb. 5 and addressed to Armed Forces chief army Gen. Nicholas de Bari Hermoza Rios.

Experts speculated the military plan was leaked to spur talks for a peaceful end to the crisis, and Fujimori called reports of a "violent entry" false, but added he would not rule out the military option if hostages were harmed.
